title: Measured tones
hook: recite the Qur'an in slow, measured rhythm (73:4)

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Muzzammil, and your line, stand in the night. Did you find two quiet minutes, before sleep or before dawn? Today, how to recite once you're standing. Day six hundred fifty-three.

Play a podcast at double speed and you'll get the information. You won't get the person. The pauses, the breath before a hard sentence, the way a voice slows down when it means something: all gone. The same verse that calls the Prophet to stand the night tells him how to recite once he's standing. And the instruction uses one root twice, in a way that sounds like what it asks for.

Verse four ends, in Pickthall's translation: "and chant the Qur'an in measure." The Arabic is wa rattili al-Qur'ana tartila. Rattil, and then tartil: the verb and its noun together, which in Arabic adds emphasis. Recite it in measure, truly in measure. Tartil means a recitation that is slow, clear, evenly spaced, each letter given its full sound. Every sound gets its own room. How did the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ actually recite? His wife Umm Salamah was asked, and according to reports in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, she described his recitation as distinct, letter by letter, pausing at the end of each verse. And Anas ibn Malik, in Sahih al-Bukhari, said he would draw out the long vowels. From verses like this one grew an entire science, tajwid, the rules for pronouncing the Qur'an correctly: where to lengthen, where to pause, how each letter is formed. It is passed on from teacher to student. Different reciting styles developed too, slower and more melodic, or plainer. But they share the measure. Why does it matter? Verse five gives a hint: We are about to send down on you a weighty word. You don't carry something heavy at a run. You carry it slowly, with your full attention. Tartil is what attention sounds like out loud. The slowness isn't a delay before the meaning. It's how the meaning gets in.

The practice: one surah, very slowly. If you know a short surah, al-Fatiha or al-Ikhlas, recite it now, in Arabic or in translation, at half your usual speed. Give every word its full sound. Pause at the end of each verse, and breathe. If you don't know one, take any line you love and say it the same way, a word at a time, as if each word were heavy. Then sit in the quiet after. The bell holds the time.
Tartil. Slow, clear, measured recitation, each letter given its room. In 73:4: rattili al-Qur'ana tartila, recite it in measure. Today's word.
Your line: slowly, measured. Today, pick one thing you'd normally rush, a prayer, a message, a sentence to someone you love, and say it at half speed. Day six hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims who learn to recite the Qur'an study tartil and the rules of tajwid with a teacher: slow, clear, with lengthened vowels and pauses at verse ends, in prayer and in daily reading.

original.note: Arabic: measured, distinct recitation, from the root r-t-l; 73:4 says rattili al-Qur'ana tartila.

trapdoor: what you thought: read the Qur'an slowly.
what it means: recite with every letter given its full sound, evenly spaced, as the Prophet did.
what a scholar hears: the cognate accusative tartila intensifies the command; Umm Salamah's description became a model, and tajwid grew from verses like this.
